content: There is significant uncertainty regarding the extent to which individuals value the proposed options. Similarly, the acceptability of the intervention to key stakeholders is uncertain. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) believes that this recommendation would be acceptable to older adults and stakeholders. Multimodal exercise aligns with the values of enhancing physical capacity and skills. Family members may also appreciate the intervention if it leads to improved mobility. However, contextual factors, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, may limit the perceived value of the intervention. Therefore, adapting the intervention to the local context may be necessary in these settings. Additional consultations with external advisory groups and the use of adaptation guides may be required to scale up interventions in culturally diverse environments. The resource requirements for implementing the intervention are uncertain. Training, especially involving the use of equipment for exercise interventions, is resource-intensive. However, the health benefits derived from the recommendation are likely to outweigh the resources needed for implementation. Cost-mitigation strategies, such as task-shifting, engaging family members, and employing a train-the-trainer model, may help reduce expenses. The feasibility of implementing the intervention is also uncertain. Some trials have involved non-specialist healthcare professionals in delivering the exercise intervention. In lowand middle-income countries, non-specialist healthcare workers or community health volunteers at the primary care or community level have been involved in delivering such public health interventions effectively. These professionals can be trained to provide care for older adults. However, whether existing staff can be utilized or whether a separate cadre of non-specialist health workers for geriatric care is needed requires further discussion with policymakers and key stakeholders. The GDG strongly believes that this recommendation will improve health equity. Adherence to physical exercise without assistance is more common among higher-income and better-educated older populations. Multimodal exercise, including progressive strength resistance training and other components such as balance, flexibility, and aerobic training, should be recommended for older adults with declining physical capacity, as measured by gait speed, grip strength, and other physical performance metrics. The strength of this recommendation is strong, and the quality of evidence is moderate. The effects and quality of evidence for stand-alone progressive resistance training and T’ai Chi were not deemed sufficient for inclusion in the recommendation. The duration of the intervention was typically 7 to 12 months, with a training frequency of three days per week being the most common. There was significant heterogeneity in the exercise components included in multimodal exercise trials. It may be important to distinguish the effect size for different combinations of exercises to provide a more accurate estimate of the intervention's effects. Most trials included in systematic reviews were conducted in high-income countries, which may limit the generalizability of the evidence to low-resource healthcare settings. The average age of older adults recruited in the evaluated trials may exceed that of the target population in lowand middle-income countries, potentially influencing the applicability of these findings to these populations. Compliance rates were found to decline in multimodal training programs that transitioned from group exercise classes with high supervision to home-based exercises. Commitment to and compliance with training programs are critical for achieving optimal benefits. Supervision by trained professionals may be necessary for high-intensity exercise and home-based training programs. Exercise programs designed for older adults with cognitive impairments should be tailored to meet individual needs and delivered with greater flexibility in a less structured manner compared to programs for older adults without cognitive impairments.
